blocks.text: In the epilogue of my book, Indonesia: Revitalization & Resitalisation Pancasila as Cita- Cita Nation (Compas, 2018), I'm opening with the story of Venezuela. The title is short:
The title was born of anxiety at that time: a scenario about Indonesia in 2030. Will Indonesia become one of the world's greatest economic forces, or will it collapse on its own internal burden?

The concern was strong after Prabowo Subianto's speech at the University of Indonesia in September 2017, which quotes the various studies of the possibility of Indonesia no longer existed in 2030. Singer and August Cole.
About this last part of the Quran.
Venezuela is giving a real illustration of how such a scenario could happen. A country can end up fighting without war enough through a massive missequence of systematic and sustainable.

The pattern is classic: the promise of well-being that turns into a putting of power, and it leads to an institutional dissolution. In December 1998, Hugo Chávez was elected President with three big promises: eliminating corruption, removing poverty and social marginalization, and establishing new order through the new constitution.

Sounds noble. But a decade later, corruption worsened, poverty still rooted, and the Constitution's constitution changed its function. It is no longer an instrument of reform, but a demolition machine for democratic institutions.
The country is personalized. Power focused. Institution is down.
When Chávez died in 2013, Nicolás Maduro inherited the power machine and operated worse.

The signs look clear in numbers. In mid 2014, the US black market exchange value jumped almost 40%, the classic signal of collapse of trust in currency and economic policy. That's just the beginning. In one generation, Venezuela had the fastest backstroke from one of the richest countries in Latin America to one of the poorest.
Venezuela Sossekol situation

One, poverty is very high. About 82 percent of the population live in poverty, more than half of it in extreme poverty. The study of Ecoanalítica (2023) shows 65% of citizens earning under US $100 a month, and only 2% above US $1,000 reflect the collapse of domestic income.

Two, hyperinflation destroys purchasing power. In 2018, Venezuela's inflation exceeded 65,000% (average of Latin America 6.7%). Even down, inflation is still three digits in 2023. Exception of continuous increase in prices, a weak policy response, and international sanctions extend the crisis cycle, eroding the ability of citizens to survive.

Three, hunger is structural. Minimum wage is only US $0.90 a month and has not gone up since 2022. Although there are benefits, public sector workers survive at about US $160 a month, private sector is US $237, while food costs surpass US $500 a month. As the AP News reports (August 27, 2025), for many families, every meal is a struggle, from fear of running out of food to not eating all day while hungry.

Four, systematic political repression. Venezuela has been ranked 156 out of the 180 on World Press Freedom Index 2024; over 115 media have been closed since the Maduro era. Until September 2024, it was recorded over 1,700 political prisoners. The Anti-Hate Act allowed punishment for up to 20 years, with extensive surveillance and dissociative campaigns; citizens are being held just for recording public events or commenting online.

Five, massive exotic. When the economy collapsed and public space was locked up, citizen response was often just one: revoke. According to UNHCR, about 8 million people (approximately 20% of the population) have left Venezuela within a decade. It's the greatest exodus of the modern era. They're not cowards. They're victims.

Venezuela is an example of the country failing to accept not because of lack of resources, even very rich in oil. It's because power is left without brakes and executed to secure elite control, not build up the capacity of the people. The country went into a locked-in economic and social instability crisis. In that vortex, ordinary citizens are always victims. Ironically, it all happened on behalf of the people.
So Venezuela is not just a Latin American story; it's a universal warning.

In the Ghost Fleet by Peter Singer and August Cole, a series of World War III between the United States and China, Indonesia was not described as a eye collapse in 2030, but had lost its strategic sovereignty. The state remains formal, but is functionally fragile: the struggle is falling through systemic loss in high-tech warfare, which is to shift from actor to arena. It's because it failed to establish human capacity, institutions and technology relevant to its time.

Ghost Fleet is not a prophecy about Indonesia, but a warning about the pattern of modern country's failure: power without brakes, pending reform, and the human foundation that is ignored. The country can lose its future without ever realizing when the turning point is passed.

This is where the slices with the analysis that I bring into light. The country doesn't end up poor because of resources, but by mishandling and transformation failure. Indonesia remains existential, but is trapped in a middle-inceme trap lower. The quality of education and innovation is left behind, institutions are not adaptive, and the elite are busier to secure control than to strengthen national capacity. Without a fundamental transformation, Indonesia could be trapped permanently.
History rarely screams. He whispers more often. But this time, the sound was clear. Time's still there. The question is one: are we willing to listen to love and make a real transformation?

The epilogue I closed with one key question: whether Indonesia 2030 will become a story of cynicism or optimism, fully determined by how far we can hug and make the Indonesian Dream rooted in Pancasila.

As I explained in the book, Indonesian Dream is a man's dream and a nation of sovereignty and justice and knowledge. It can only be built through strengthening three essential capital: spiritual capital, social capital, and human capital.
Among the three, it's the most fragile of human capital today. And that's where the future of the true nation is determined.
